source_text: Σύγκρισις τῶν παραβολῶν ἐν αἷς Θεὸς ἄνθρωπος καλεῖται. Ἐν μὲν τῇ τῶν ἐργατῶν πατὴρ οἰκογενὴς ἔξεισι μισθώσασθαι· ἐν δὲ τῇ τοῦ δείπνου καὶ τῶν γάμων τοῦ υἱοῦ βασιλεὺς ὠνόμασται — μείζων γὰρ πατρὸς οἰκογενοῦς ὡς στρατιὰν πέμπων. Παρὰ Λουκᾷ «ἄνθρωπος ἐφύτευσεν ἀμπελῶνα»· καὶ παρὰ Μάρκῳ ὁμοίως. Πολλαχῶς ἐν ταῖς Γραφαῖς ὁ Θεὸς ἄνθρωπος λαμβάνεται· πολὺ διαφέρει εἰ ἁπλῶς ἄνθρωπος ἢ οἰκοδεσπότης ἢ βασιλεὺς ὀνομάζεται. Δόξα Χριστῷ. Ἀμήν.
thought_title: Comparison of parables where God is called a man
orientation: Origen is closing his treatment of the parable of the vineyard by comparing how God is depicted as a human figure in different Gospel parables.
pass_a_gloss: Comparison of the parables in which God [is] called man. In [the] one of the workers [a] father [of a] household goes out to hire; in [the] one of the dinner and of the weddings of the son [he] has been named king — greater for than [a] father [of a] household as [an] army sending. In Luke "[a] man planted [a] vineyard"; and in Mark likewise. In many ways in the Scriptures [the] God [as] man is taken; much [it] differs if simply [a] man or [a] master of [a] house or [a] king [he] is named. Glory [to] Christ. Amen.

choices.why: οἰκογενής means one who is master of a house, not a slave born in the house; the father is the householder who goes out to hire workers.

choices.english: for he is greater than a father who is a householder
choices.why: The comparison is between the king and the father-householder; the king is greater because he sends an army, not merely hires workers.
The king's greatness is shown by his sending an army, a mark of royal authority beyond a householder's hiring.
In the sense of 'is understood' or 'is received' as a man in the Scriptures; the passive voice is preserved.
The impersonal construction emphasizes the distinction between the titles applied to God.

bible_refs.note: παρὰ Μάρκῳ ὁμοίως, referring to the same parable wording

pass_b_english: A comparison of the parables in which God is called a man. In the parable of the workers, a father who is a householder goes out to hire. In the parable of the dinner and the weddings of the son, he has been named a king—for he is greater than a father who is a householder, as one sending an army. In Luke, "a man planted a vineyard" (Luke 20:9); and in Mark likewise. In many ways in the Scriptures God is taken as a man; it makes a great difference whether he is named simply a man, or a householder, or a king. Glory to Christ. Amen.

last_rejected.why: Greek has singular 'wedding' (γάμων gen. pl. but refers to one wedding feast), not 'weddings'
last_rejected.ruling: γάμων is genitive plural 'weddings'; English correctly renders the Greek form. Claim that it refers to one wedding is interpretive, not a translation error.

last_rejected.why: στρατιὰν means 'army' but context shows it's 'retinue' or 'servants'; king sends servants, not military army
last_rejected.ruling: στρατιὰν means 'army'; 'as one sending an army' is literal and accurate. 'Retinue' is a softer gloss but not required.
